pq01.d1: Shawn hosts the weekly review; the decision log lives in the runbook. Every Friday Shawn walks through the week's changes, and the hosting notes get a dedicated section when infrastructure topics come up. The runbook holds the decision log: each entry records what was chosen, who was present, and the date, so future engineers can trace why the system looks the way it does. Shawn insists the log stay current; a stale entry is worse than none, because it sends readers down the wrong path. The review also covers the hosting cost sheet, flagging any host whose spend drifts above its tag. Action items from the review land in the tracker before the meeting ends, and Shawn reads them back aloud to confirm ownership.
pq01.d2: The deploy will decide which hosts fail the check; Shawn pulls them from rotation. During the rollout, each host runs a health probe, and the deploy controller decides whether the host stays or goes based on the probe result. Shawn watches the dashboard as hosts flip from green to red; any host that fails the check gets pulled from rotation immediately, before it can serve traffic. The decision is automatic, but Shawn keeps a hand on the control in case the probe itself is faulty. Hosts that pass rejoin the pool, and the deploy continues. The log records every decide-and-pull event with a timestamp, so the team can audit which hosts were cut and why. Shawn reviews the log after each deploy to spot flaky hosts.
pq01.d3: Shawn will decide to host the birthday dinner at the lake house this year. The guest list is still open, and Shawn wants to decide the final headcount before ordering food. Hosting at the lake house means arranging boats, bedding, and a backup plan for rain. Shawn asked everyone to reply by Friday so he can decide whether the main room fits all the guests or the party spills onto the deck. The lake house host provides the grill, and Shawn will bring the cake. Last year the dinner ran late, so this year Shawn plans to decide the seating early and keep the speeches short. Everyone agrees the lake house beats a restaurant, and Shawn is glad to host.
pq01.d4: Which host does the canary target? Shawn will decide the staging host first. The canary deploy needs a single host to absorb the new build before the fleet follows. Shawn will decide which staging host takes the canary by checking current load; the quietest host wins. Once the canary host reports healthy, Shawn gives the signal and the deploy fans out. If the canary host stumbles, Shawn decides to roll back and the fleet never sees the bad build. The decision log notes which host served as canary each time, building a history of reliable targets. Shawn prefers to rotate the canary host so no single machine bears every test. Hosting the canary on staging keeps production untouched until the build proves itself.
pq01.d5: Shawn keeps the hosting cost sheet; every host gets a tag before he will decide. The sheet tracks each host's monthly spend, and Shawn reviews it when deciding whether to keep, resize, or retire a machine. Every host gets a tag naming its owner and purpose before Shawn will decide its fate; untagged hosts get flagged in red. Hosting costs crept up last quarter, so Shawn decided to audit the tags and found three hosts nobody claimed. He decided to shut them down, saving a noticeable sum. The sheet now updates automatically, but Shawn still eyeballs it weekly. Deciding where to host a new service starts with the sheet: Shawn picks the cheapest host with headroom.
pq01.gold: The Hub will be hosted on Cloudflare Workers. The Workers platform runs code at the edge, close to users, which keeps latency low for the dashboard and the API. Hosting there means no servers to provision and no containers to orchestrate; a push to the main branch triggers a fresh deploy in under a minute. The team evaluated several platforms before settling, and Workers won on cold-start speed and the simplicity of the bindings for KV storage. Static assets sit on Pages, while the dynamic routes run as Workers. The runbook documents the rollback path: every deploy keeps the prior version warm for instant reversion. Cost scales with requests, so idle nights cost nothing. The choice is now recorded as settled, and the infrastructure notes point new engineers at the Workers dashboard first.

pq03.d1: Fourteen questions were drafted for the quiz; the question bank was derived from last year's test. The quiz team derived fourteen questions from last year's test, keeping the difficulty curve intact. Each question was derived by rewording a prior item, so the bank feels familiar but not repeated. Fourteen new questions joined the bank this cycle, and the derived items were tagged by topic. The team checks that no question was derived twice from the same source, which would make the quiz lopsided. Derived questions go through a review where two editors confirm the wording is clear. The fourteen-question set ships to the quiz engine on Friday.
pq03.d2: The derived step runs fourteen times; all questions are logged nightly. In the pipeline, the derived step runs fourteen times, once per shard, and all questions are logged nightly to the audit table. Each derived run processes fourteen questions, and the log records which questions appeared in which shard. The derived step is idempotent, so running it fourteen times is safe even if a shard retries. Questions that fail validation are logged separately, and the derived output skips them. Fourteen is the shard count, not a limit — the step scales by adding shards. The nightly log lets the team confirm all fourteen questions were covered.
pq03.d3: Fourteen interns derived the survey questions from the question template. The survey team hired fourteen interns, and each intern derived questions from the question template for a different audience segment. The derived questions were collected into a shared bank, where duplicates were merged. Fourteen interns working in parallel derived the full set in a week. Each derived question cites the template section it came from, so reviewers can trace the lineage. The interns derived fourteen questions each, then swapped segments to cross-check. Questions that survived review were marked derived-and-approved.
pq03.d4: The derived policy asks question fourteen of the fourteen questions above. Under the derived policy, the reviewer asks question fourteen of the fourteen questions above, then records the answer. The fourteen questions are numbered, and the derived policy specifies the order: question fourteen comes after thirteen, as listed. Each derived review covers all fourteen questions, and the answers feed the derived report. The policy was derived from the audit findings, which showed reviewers skipping questions. Now the derived checklist requires all fourteen, and question fourteen — the attestation — cannot be skipped. Derived policies are versioned, so question fourteen's wording is pinned.
pq03.d5: The fourteen derived metrics feed the questions dashboard every night; run the check nightly. The dashboard shows fourteen derived metrics, and the questions panel refreshes every night from the derived tables. Each derived metric is computed from the questions log, so the dashboard reflects what was actually asked. The fourteen metrics include counts, and the derived pipeline runs the check nightly to catch gaps. Questions that never appear get flagged, and the derived metrics highlight them in red. The team reviews the fourteen derived numbers each morning, then runs the check nightly to keep them fresh.
pq03.gold: The fourteen questions re-derive every run; answers are never carried. Each run starts fresh: the fourteen questions are posed anew, and the answers from the previous run are discarded, never carried forward. This keeps the questions honest, because a carried answer would anchor the next run to old thinking. The cadence is every run, without exception — the questions do not persist across runs. Fourteen is the fixed count; the set does not grow or shrink. Teams that tried to reuse answers found the questions went stale, so the rule is now strict: re-derive, do not recall. The questions live in the activation packet, and each run reads them cold.

pq07.d1: The feeder stalls when the queue backs up; drain it by hand. When the feeder stalls, the queue backs up behind it, and the only fix is to drain it by hand. The feeder's intake clogs, the queue depth climbs, and the alarm fires. Draining by hand means opening the panel and clearing the feeder throat, then watching the queue drain down. The feeder resumes once the queue is clear. To avoid the stall, the team drains the feeder on a schedule, keeping the queue shallow. A backed-up queue starves downstream, so the feeder's health is checked hourly.
pq07.d2: Drain the queue before the feeder restarts. The restart procedure is strict: drain the queue before the feeder restarts, or the feeder will jam on the backlog. Draining the queue takes a few minutes; the feeder waits in standby. Once the queue is empty, the feeder restarts cleanly and pulls fresh items. The runbook says to drain the queue fully — a partial drain leaves the feeder chewing on stale items. After the feeder restarts, the queue refills gradually. The team drains the queue before every feeder restart, no exceptions.
pq07.d3: The queue drains slowly; the feeder waits. When the downstream consumer lags, the queue drains slowly and the feeder waits for room. The feeder cannot push into a full queue, so it idles while the queue drains. A slowly draining queue is normal during peak, and the feeder is designed to wait patiently. The queue drains through a narrow pipe, which is why the feeder waits instead of forcing items in. Operators watch the queue depth; if the feeder waits too long, they drain the queue manually to unblock it.
pq07.d4: Feeder logs show the queue never drained. The overnight feeder logs show the queue never drained; the drain valve stayed shut all night. Feeder telemetry confirms the queue depth never dropped, which means nothing was drained. The team suspects the feeder's drain signal never fired. Logs from the feeder show repeated drain attempts, but the queue never drained. Until the feeder actually drains the queue, the backlog keeps growing. The fix is to cycle the feeder and watch the queue drain on the next attempt.
pq07.d5: A full queue stops the feeder cold. When the queue fills completely, the feeder halts; there is nowhere for the next item to go. The feeder's sensor trips at ninety percent, but a sudden surge can fill the queue before the feeder reacts. A stopped feeder means the intake backs up, so the team watches queue depth closely. The feeder restarts automatically once the queue has room, pulling items at its normal pace. To keep the feeder moving, the consumer must keep up with the queue. A full queue is the most common reason the feeder stops.
pq07.gold: Drained items land in the digest each night. The digest is a nightly summary: every item that was drained during the day lands there, timestamped and grouped by source. Drained items stay in the digest for thirty days, then age out. The digest goes to the team each morning, so everyone sees what was drained overnight. If a drained item looks wrong, the digest links back to the original record for review. The nightly drain is the only writer to the digest; nothing else lands there. Drained items that fail validation are held out of the digest and flagged separately.

pq09.d1: The merge gates on the lint check. In this repo, the merge gates on the lint check: no branch merges until lint is clean. The lint check runs first, and the merge gate watches its status. If the lint check fails, the merge is blocked and the gate stays red. The team added the lint check to the merge gates after a bad deploy slipped through. Now every merge must clear the lint check, and the gate enforces it. The check is fast, so the merge gate rarely slows anyone down. Gating the merge on lint caught three real bugs last month.
pq09.d2: Which gates does the merge check cover in the new pipeline? The new pipeline added gates, and the merge check now covers them all. The merge check walks the list of gates: lint, tests, security scan, and the receipt check. Each gate must pass before the merge check gives the green light. The pipeline's merge gates are configured in one file, so adding a gate is a single-line change. The merge check reports which gate failed, if any. Teams like that the merge check covers every gate, because nothing slips through. The new pipeline's gates have cut bad merges to zero.
pq09.d3: The check gates every merge to main. The policy is simple: the check gates every merge to main, without exception. The merge queue processes branches in order, and the check gates each one. A merge that skips the check is rejected by the gate. The check itself is quick, so gating every merge to main adds only seconds. The team trusts the main branch because the check gates it so strictly. Every merge to main passes through the same check and the same gates. The gate log shows every merge the check approved.
pq09.d4: Merge first, then the gates check the diff. This team's flow is unusual: merge first, then the gates check the diff after the fact. The merge lands, and then the gates run their checks on the merged code. If a gate's check fails post-merge, the team reverts. Merging first keeps velocity high, and the gates check everything within minutes. The check suite covers the diff thoroughly, so post-merge gates catch issues fast. Some teams gate before merging, but here the merge comes first and the gates check second. The diff check is the same either way.
pq09.d5: The gated check blocks the merge. The gated check is the strictest one: it blocks the merge until every condition is met. The merge waits while the gated check runs its full suite. If the gated check finds a problem, the merge is blocked and the author is notified. The team relies on the gated check to block bad merges before they land. Unblocking requires the gated check to pass on a fresh run. The merge gate delegates to the gated check, which has the final say. Blocking the merge is the gated check's entire job.
pq09.gold: The receipt check must pass before merging. The receipt check verifies that every required artifact is attached: the diff, the test log, and the reviewer sign-off. No check is skipped; the receipt check fails if any artifact is missing. The check runs automatically when the pull request is opened, and it re-runs on every push. A passing receipt check turns the status green, which is the signal the team waits for. The check takes about two minutes, scanning the attached files for completeness. If the receipt check fails, the author gets a list of what's missing. The check is the last step before the branch can move forward.
